## Introduction and approve agenda

This was the first TSC meeting since Rodrigo took over as chair and Douglas as vice-chair on September 1. Rodrigo noted the agenda was packed and aimed to move through it quickly.

## Review action items from previous meeting

### How to handle security notifications ([discussion #331](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/tsc/discussions/331))

Rodrigo has written up a proposal for notifying the people responsible for an algorithm implementation when a new vulnerability is reported. It would informally group the responsible people and notify them through their GitHub accounts, leaving each person to choose how that notification reaches them (a GitHub notification, an email to the associated address, and so on). He asked members to comment on the discussion. If there is agreement, he will set it up and contact the responsible party for each implementation to collect their GitHub handle, where it is not already known, and to confirm they are happy with this approach. No one commented in the meeting.

### Review guidelines ([PR #332](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/tsc/pull/332))

Rodrigo has posted a short, simple set of review guidelines, following the TSC's earlier discussions on review quality. He asked members to read the PR (it is not a long read) and either comment or approve it. He will merge it once there are enough approvals.

### Caretaker approach ([PR #333](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/tsc/pull/333))

Rodrigo has formalized the caretaker role discussed at the last TSC meeting and at status meetings: someone who steps in on a subproject that has no maintainers or committers. The PR sets out how a caretaker is approved, what their responsibilities are and are not, and how a subproject moves from caretaker status to formal maintenance. He expects this item to need more careful discussion than the other two. Michael has already commented and some of those comments are still being worked through. Rodrigo asked members to review the PR and weigh in.

Douglas thanked Rodrigo for putting the three items together and said he will give feedback. Rodrigo added that he is also drafting guidelines for algorithm inclusion, but will publish them only after these three are settled, so that there are not too many discussions open at once.

## Round 3 on-ramp update

### Submission teams

The August 31 round 3 deadline has passed. Rodrigo reported that all of the new submission teams want their algorithm included in liboqs, and all want to take part in the inclusion work in some way. His plan is to invite each team to a separate status meeting, walk them through the inclusion process and discuss blockers specific to their implementation:

- **SDitH** joined the [September 8 status meeting](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/tsc/blob/main/oqs-status-meetings/2026-09-08%20-%20OQS%20status%20meeting%20-%20summary.md).
- **QR-UOV** is being invited for September 29.
- **FAEST** is being invited for October 6 (not yet confirmed).

This would mean all of the new teams have joined a status meeting by the first week of October. For QR-UOV, at least three people outside the submission team have offered to help with inclusion, which has not happened for the other algorithms.

### `copy_from_upstream`

Bruce has no significant updates on the `copy_from_upstream` refactor. Round 3 inclusion will use `copy_from_upstream` as it is today. He will try to approve quickly any PRs from community members or maintainers with small bug fixes or documentation clarifications.

### Round 2 candidates already in liboqs

Of the four round 2 candidates already in liboqs that advanced to round 3, three have had their round 3 updates merged: [UOV](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2554), [MQOM](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2563) and [MAYO](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2564). The [SNOVA round 3 update (PR #2562)](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2562) is still pending.

Michael stressed that looking after algorithms already in liboqs should come first. The SNOVA PR is blocking downstream work: oqs-provider has its round 3 updates ready ([PR #830](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/830)) but they cannot be merged until the liboqs change is in. Rodrigo added that the provider's 0.12.0 release should go out before that merge. Bruce said he is giving the SNOVA review priority. His review found some minor build configuration issues, and the submission team has replied that these are easy to fix. Once they are fixed and CI passes, he expects it to be ready to merge.

Basil asked about the fourth round 2 candidate, CROSS, which was not selected for round 3. Rodrigo has an email to write to the CROSS team asking about their plans before any decision on deprecation. Michael pointed out that a GitHub issue already exists where he told the CROSS team that CROSS would be removed if OQS did not hear from them. The team replied that they are looking at other standardization venues and will post an update there. He asked that the conversation stay on GitHub so the issue does not go stale. Rodrigo had not seen that reply; he will read it and follow up.

### New symmetric primitives

Two of the new schemes need symmetric primitives that liboqs's common code does not yet provide:

- **Rijndael-256.** MQOM already uses Rijndael-256 and carries its own copy, and SDitH needs it too. Bruce proposed moving it into common code but does not want this to block SDitH. The next major release is some way off, so SDitH can be merged with its own copy for now. Once there is a mature implementation, or one built on the existing AES code, Rijndael-256 can be moved into common code with the same shimming used for SHA-3 and AES. Rodrigo agreed, with one caveat: OpenSSL does not expose Rijndael-256, which Norm confirmed, so the OpenSSL-backed option will not be available and liboqs will have to rely on its own implementation.
- **AES-192.** FAEST needs AES-192. Norm has opened [PR #2571](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2571) (for [issue #2570](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2570)), which takes AES-192 from the same sources as the existing AES-128 and AES-256 implementations, for consistency. Michael asked whether OpenSSL could simply be used. Norm and Rodrigo explained that AES-192 is handled exactly like AES-128 and AES-256: builds configured to use OpenSSL get it from OpenSSL, and native implementations (such as ARM) are also provided. The PR therefore does add code for OQS to maintain.

### SDitH

Rodrigo expects SDitH inclusion to need substantial restructuring rather than minor changes, because of how its code is organized. He tried using Claude to refactor it last week without getting far, and has opened a discussion on [issue #2453](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2453). He would like the OQS side to agree on an approach first and then propose it to the team, including how the work would be split. Basil has not yet looked at the code in detail. He suggested the common-code facility in `copy_from_upstream` might work for SDitH, but has not checked.

Bruce has spent the past week on this. SDitH selects parameters at runtime, so instead of changing its internals, the liboqs API can be wrapped around it: pass in the parameters at runtime and route its entropy requests through OQS random bytes. This matches the approach in Rodrigo's Claude-assisted summary on the issue. Bruce already has a first working implementation, and he will bring a proposal once everything works. Bruce and Owen will lead SDitH integration. Bruce wanted to make sure the SDitH team knows this so work is not duplicated. Following Michael's point, they will say so on the GitHub issue.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Bruce / Owen):** Comment on [issue #2453](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2453) that they will drive SDitH integration, and post the wrapper-based proposal there or at next week's status meeting.

> **Action (Basil):** Look at the SDitH code base and comment on [issue #2453](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2453) on how hard inclusion is likely to be.

## Planification for upcoming conferences

In a few weeks, Open Source Summit Europe and then the OpenSSL Conference take place in Prague, a week apart. Rodrigo is speaking at the Open Source Summit, and Michael and Norm are speaking at the OpenSSL Conference.

### Messages to convey

Rodrigo's talk is a general Open Quantum Safe talk rather than one on a specific topic. Its purpose is to present OQS's continuing mission and current work, such as round 3 algorithm inclusion, and to bring in new contributors or win back people who have lost interest. He also plans to talk to Hart about a short interactive poll, shared by QR code, to gather feedback on what people like about OQS and what they would like to see, similar to a past PQCA poll.

- **Call to action.** Douglas suggested leaving the audience with a clear call to action covering both what OQS can do for them and, especially, what OQS would like them to do. Norm agreed and added that OQS should decide concretely what help it is asking for and be ready if people take it up. Michael agreed and suggested working this out in a GitHub issue, possibly an internal one, so everyone can contribute. Rodrigo will think about it and bring ideas to a status meeting.
- **Sister projects.** Douglas also suggested a slide on the wider PQCA ecosystem: PQ Code Package, with its high-quality implementations of the standardized algorithms, and the new PQCA project Longfellow.

Michael warned that this could be politically sensitive at the OpenSSL Conference. Promoting faster PQ Code Package implementations will invite the question of why they have not been contributed to OpenSSL. He noted he had pointed PQ Code Package developers to an OpenSSL request for optimized ML-KEM and ML-DSA, and that his own provider exposing ML-DSA through OpenSSL shows much better performance. Douglas disagreed that this was a fair summary of the discussions about a relationship that took place about a year and a half ago. In his view, saying that other implementations exist and are useful for different purposes is not an attack, OpenSSL is also the right choice for many users, and the TSC does not need to relitigate this. Michael said he was not speaking for OpenSSL. He considers the issue still unresolved and a sore point, and said speakers should be prepared for the question.

Hart said the PQCA has done much of the legal groundwork, so there is now a clear route for contributing code to OpenSSL. What is needed is for OpenSSL to want the code and for all contributors to the relevant modules to sign the OpenSSL contributor license agreement. Gathering those signatures will take some wrangling, but he hopes it will not be burdensome. He suggested answering the question by saying PQCA is happy to work with OpenSSL to make it happen. Rodrigo said his talk will focus on Open Quantum Safe. He does not speak for the mlkem-native or mldsa-native teams, so if asked he will say that this is a matter between those implementers and OpenSSL, and pass on Hart's message.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Rodrigo):** Define a concrete call to action (what help OQS is asking for, and how people can take it up) for the conference talks, and open a GitHub issue for input.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Rodrigo):** Talk to Hart about running an interactive feedback poll during the talks.

## Security response process

Rodrigo estimated that roughly 51 items are open in the [security-tracking](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/security-tracking) repository. Some concern algorithms maintained by submission teams or others outside OQS. Those will be handled once the notification process from [discussion #331](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/tsc/discussions/331) is in place, after which responsibility passes to the relevant parties. Others belong to OQS, and roughly half of all items (about 28–32) concern the stateful signatures (LMS/XMSS), where Norm is taking the lead.

Douglas said Bruce has been working through some advisories, but OQS is still overwhelmed. The tracking repository gathers everything in one place, but the fixes still have to be done. Part of the volume appears to be repeat reports of known, unresolved problems, and it is hard to tell new reports from repeats. Clearing the older items should therefore slow the intake. He said help is needed. He has fallen behind and will get back to it next week, once the term is well underway.

Norm has worked on the LMS/XMSS items he knew about two or three weeks ago, including some duplicates between the Trail of Bits findings and another source, and believed he had addressed the related PRs. He has not seen any newer reports. He plans to respond to one recent issue, which was reported as an API contract violation rather than a security issue. Rodrigo asked Norm to go through the tracking repository and group the LMS/XMSS items that are really the same problem, so the TSC knows how many distinct issues remain and can plan the work. Douglas pointed to [security-tracking issue #65](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/security-tracking/issues/65), a meta-issue summarizing the LMS/HSS cluster. It needs updating with reports received since it was written, and the aim is to get the first batch of fixes from that cluster out. Douglas will follow up with Norm later in the week.

**CVEs.** An earlier blocker was that GitHub has been slow to assign CVEs. Two advisories have been ready to publish for about a month with no CVE from GitHub. Douglas proposed publishing them as GitHub Security Advisories (GHSAs) without CVE numbers and asked for opinions. Rodrigo said oqs-provider has been doing the same with its roughly eight advisories this year, and that the same is happening on the liboqs side. He added that AI is clearly having an impact on report volume, not always a positive one. No one objected.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Norm / Douglas):** Meet later this week to update [security-tracking issue #65](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/security-tracking/issues/65) with newer reports, group the LMS/XMSS items that are really the same problem, and get the first batch of fixes out.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Douglas):** Publish the two ready liboqs advisories as GHSAs without waiting further for CVE numbers.
